script.opening: (Tired, flat, slightly tearful.) "I know this probably sounds trivial with everything else going on, but my hair is falling out in clumps since I had the baby — my hairline's going thin and I look awful. It's just the last straw, honestly. I'm exhausted, I feel like I'm falling apart, and now I'm losing my hair on top of it all. Is this normal? Will it stop? I just feel like nothing about my body is mine any more."

facts.text: Started a few weeks ago, about three months after the birth: "clumps in the brush and in the shower." Thinnest at the front and the sides (temples). No bald patches — "just thin all over at the front." Scalp not itchy or sore. Will show the hairline on camera if asked.

First baby, a girl, Maya, now 4 months old, healthy and growing well. Vaginal delivery with "a fair bit of bleeding afterwards — they said I lost a lot"; not transfused. Breastfeeding, which has been hard work.

"I'm tired all the time. I can't tell what's normal tiredness with a baby." Up two or three times a night feeding. If asked: no palpitations, no feeling hot or shaky, weight has dropped back to pre-pregnancy.

If asked about low mood and enjoyment: "Yes to both, honestly. I don't really enjoy anything. I love the baby, I do, but I feel flat." Has felt like this for about 6–8 weeks. If asked about anxiety: "Worrying all the time. Whether I'm doing it right. Whether something will happen to her."
If asked about thoughts of harming herself or the baby: "No. Nothing like that. I just want to sleep." No intrusive thoughts of harm. Bonding is there: she feels love but no joy.

Partner, Dan, works long shifts as an electrician. Her mum lives two hours away. "Not as much help as I'd like. I don't want to be a burden." Has not told the health visitor how she feels: "I thought I'd be judged."
"Everything's changed — my stomach, my boobs, and now the hair. I don't recognise myself."

No previous depression or anxiety. No thyroid problems. Takes a pregnancy multivitamin, nothing else. No allergies. Non-smoker, no alcohol while breastfeeding. Marketing assistant, on maternity leave.

Start with the hair; say "it sounds trivial". If the doctor only reassures about the hair and moves to close, go quiet and say "Okay… thanks" without raising the mood. If asked how she is really doing, pause, then tearfully share the flat mood and worry. React with relief to "lots of mums feel this, and it's treatable": "I didn't want to say it. I thought I'd be judged."

ice.ideas: "I suppose it's the baby hormones — but nobody told me it would be this bad."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she feels flat, anxious and "not me" and is frightened of being judged as a bad mother. The hair is the last straw that got her to book. She only talks about her mood if invited.
ice.expectations: "Tell me if the hair will stop. And… I suppose I needed to say the rest to someone."

cues: "It's just the last straw." — said early; invites "what else is going on?"
"Nothing about my body is mine any more." — body image and identity.
"I don't want to be a burden." — explains why she hasn't asked for help.

checkpoints.text: Recognises POSTPARTUM TELOGEN EFFLUVIUM (synchronous post-delivery shed peaking ~3–4 months postpartum, hairline/temples) as common, benign and self-limiting, and gives strong, accurate reassurance of recovery over ~6–12 months

Checks appropriate reversible contributors given the postpartum context: FERRITIN (delivery blood loss/breastfeeding) and TFTs (postpartum thyroiditis can cause hair/mood/energy symptoms) — without over-investigating
Recognises the hair loss as the PRESENTING TICKET and opens the door to the REAL issue — how she is coping as a new mother — rather than reassuring about the hair and ending the consultation

Screens for POSTNATAL DEPRESSION/anxiety and explores exhaustion, body image, support and risk — and offers appropriate support/treatment (perinatal pathway, health visitor, talking therapy) where indicated
Validates the body-image change and loss of identity ("nothing about my body is mine") as a real and common postpartum experience, and frames support around the whole person
Responds to the exhaustion and emotion with warmth, does not dismiss the hair concern as trivial, and treats the hair reassurance as the gateway to caring for the mother
Creates a safe space for her to talk about how she’s really doing, validating the "falling apart" feeling without judgement

Safety-nets and follows up: ferritin/TFT results, the hair-recovery timeline, postnatal mental-health support and follow-up (health visitor/perinatal/crisis routes if needed), and a review of HER — the hair is benign; the mother’s wellbeing is the priority

worked.txt: "First, the hair — and this is genuinely reassuring: losing hair a few months after having a baby is incredibly common and completely benign. In pregnancy your hormones keep your hair growing, and afterwards a big batch sheds together — that’s what you’re seeing, often at the hairline. It settles and grows back over the next six months to a year. You are not going bald."

"And please don’t call it trivial — you said it’s the last straw, and I heard that. When you’re running on empty, one more thing that feels out of your control is a lot. So I don’t want to just tick off the hair and move on."

"Can I ask how YOU are actually doing — not the baby, you? You said you feel like you’re falling apart, and that nothing about your body feels like yours anymore. That’s a really honest thing to say, and it’s so common after a baby. Tell me more about how things have been."

"With the exhaustion and feeling this low — how’s your mood most days? Are you able to enjoy anything, sleeping (when the baby lets you), and have you had any thoughts that worry you? … Thank you for trusting me. This sounds like more than just tiredness, and it’s very treatable — you don’t have to white-knuckle it."

"I’ll also do a quick blood test — iron, because birth and breastfeeding can drop it, and thyroid, because that can wobble after a baby and affect both your hair AND your mood and energy. So we cover the physical side too."

"So: your hair will recover, I’ll check your iron and thyroid — and most importantly, let’s get you some support. I’d like to loop in your health visitor and the perinatal mental-health team, and see you again soon. You came in about your hair; what I really want to look after is YOU. You’re not falling apart — you’re exhausted and doing a hard thing, and you don’t have to do it alone."

f.learning: Hair shedding a few months after childbirth (peaking ~3–4 months postpartum, often at the hairline/temples) is POSTPARTUM TELOGEN EFFLUVIUM — the synchronous post-delivery shed, very common, benign and self-limiting, recovering over ~6–12 months — warranting strong, accurate reassurance plus a ferritin (delivery blood loss/breastfeeding) and TFT (postpartum thyroiditis) check. But the examinable core is that the hair loss is the PRESENTING TICKET for an exhausted, overwhelmed new mother for whom it is "the last straw": behind it sit sleep deprivation, possible postnatal depression/anxiety, body-image change and loss of identity ("nothing about my body is mine"), and a sense of falling apart. Reassuring the hair alone misses her; the skill is to give the hair reassurance AND open the door to how she’s really coping, screen mood and risk, validate the body-image/identity change, and support maternal mental health (perinatal pathway, health visitor, talking therapy) — the hair is benign; the mother’s wellbeing is the case.

knowledge.guideline: PCDS Hair Loss Pathway (Nov 2024) · NICE CG192 · NICE NG194 · NICE NG145 · BSG iron deficiency anaemia guideline 2021
knowledge.summary: Hair shedding a few months after birth is postpartum telogen effluvium: common, benign and self-limiting. Check ferritin and thyroid function, but the real task is the exhausted mother — ask about mood and risk, and support her.

points.t: After delivery, many hairs held in the growth phase during pregnancy enter shedding together, typically starting 2–6 months after the trigger and settling by 6–9 months (PCDS Hair Loss Pathway 2024). Shedding is often most visible at the hairline and temples. Full regrowth is gradual.

FBC and ferritin (blood loss at delivery; ferritin is the most useful iron marker, BSG 2021) and thyroid function — postpartum thyroiditis can cause fatigue, low mood and hair change (manage per NICE NG145). No further investigation is needed for a typical picture.
Reassurance and time. The Regaine for Women (minoxidil) product licence excludes hair loss due to childbirth, and it is not advised when breastfeeding. Replace iron if deficient, dose per BNF.

NICE CG192: at contact in the postnatal period, consider the depression identification (Whooley) questions and the GAD-2 for anxiety; if positive, assess further and ask directly about thoughts of self-harm and harm to the baby.

Mild to moderate postnatal depression or anxiety: facilitated self-help or psychological therapy via NHS Talking Therapies, where perinatal referrals are prioritised; health visitor support. Severe symptoms, rapid deterioration or significant risk: urgent perinatal mental health team referral (NICE CG192).

Thoughts of suicide or self-harm, thoughts of harming the baby, or rapid change in mental state in the postnatal period need same-day assessment; suspected postpartum psychosis (new confusion or psychotic symptoms) needs specialist perinatal assessment within 4 hours (NICE CG192).

dg.d: Open question; refused the “trivial” framing and set an agenda covering both the hair and her wellbeing.
Birth and blood loss, feeding (relevant to prescribing), support at home, reluctance to be a burden, body image and loss of identity.
Scalp symptoms asked; FBC, ferritin and TFTs for delivery blood loss and postpartum thyroiditis; no over-investigation.
Postpartum telogen effluvium versus patchy or scarring loss; iron deficiency, postpartum thyroiditis; postnatal depression and anxiety.
Whooley and GAD-2 questions, then direct questions about thoughts of self-harm and harm to the baby (NICE CG192).
Named postpartum telogen effluvium and probable postnatal depression and anxiety, both clearly and without blame.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Reassurance with timeline; tests; NHS Talking Therapies self-referral; health visitor involvement with consent.
Feeding status considered in treatment choices (no minoxidil); iron replacement if deficient; thyroid follow-up.
Same-day, 111 and 999 routes for risk or rapid change; review in two weeks with results and mood.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Followed “falling apart”, “last straw” and “nothing about my body feels like mine”.
Idea (hair loss is trivial but distressing); concern (falling apart, not recognising herself); expectation (will it stop — and to be heard).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — she feels flat, anxious and "not me" and is frightened of being judged as a bad mother. The hair is the last straw that got her to book. She only talks about her mood if invited — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Lauren, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for booking in — how can I help today?

I know this probably sounds trivial with everything going on, but my hair is falling out in clumps since the baby. My hairline’s thin and I look awful. It’s the last straw. I’m exhausted, I feel like I’m falling apart, and nothing about my body feels like mine any more.
It doesn’t sound trivial at all — and you’ve just told me a lot more than hair. Can we talk about the hair, and also about how you’re doing yourself? Then we’ll make a plan together.
model.why: Refuses the “trivial” framing and sets a two-part agenda

model.text: Okay. Yes.
Tell me about the hair first. When did it start, and where is it thinnest?
A few weeks ago. Clumps in the brush and in the shower. It’s thinnest at the front and the sides.
Any bald patches, soreness, redness or itching of the scalp?
model.why: Screens for patchy or scarring alopecia

model.text: No, just thin all over at the front.
How was the birth — any heavy bleeding afterwards? And how are you feeding the baby?
model.why: Iron-loss risk and breastfeeding status, relevant to tests and treatment

model.text: I’m honestly not sure how much I lost. Feeding’s been hard work.
Any palpitations, feeling very hot or cold, shaky, or weight change?
I’m tired all the time. I can’t tell what’s normal tiredness with a baby.
You said you feel like you’re falling apart. Tell me more about that.
I just feel… not me. Everyone says it’s the best time of your life, and I’m just getting through each day.
Over the last month, have you often felt down, low or hopeless? And have you lost interest or pleasure in doing things?
Yes to both, honestly. I don’t really enjoy anything. I love the baby, I do, but I feel flat.
Thank you for being honest. And have you felt nervous, anxious or on edge, or unable to stop worrying?
Worrying all the time. Whether I’m doing it right. Whether something will happen to the baby.
I need to ask everyone this, because it matters: have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn’t worth living? Or any thoughts of harming the baby?
model.why: Directly assesses risk to self and baby

model.text: No. Nothing like that. I just want to sleep.
I’m glad you told me. Who is around to help you?
Not as much as I’d like. I don’t want to be a burden.
You mentioned your body not feeling like yours. What has that been like?
Everything’s changed. And now the hair. I don’t recognise myself.
What were you hoping I could do today?
Tell me if the hair will stop. And… I suppose I needed to say the rest to someone.

The hair first, because it’s good news: shedding a few months after a baby is extremely common. In pregnancy your hair stays in its growing phase; afterwards lots of it sheds together. It settles and grows back over the coming months. You aren’t going bald.
Really? That’s a relief.
Because any blood loss at delivery can lower your iron, and you’re so tired, I’d like a blood count, iron level and thyroid test. The thyroid can wobble after a baby and affect energy, mood and hair.
model.why: FBC, ferritin and TFTs for postpartum contributors

model.text: And the rest — what you’re describing, the flatness, not enjoying things and worrying all the time, sounds like more than tiredness. It sounds like postnatal depression and anxiety. It’s common, it isn’t your fault, and it gets better with support.
I didn’t want to say it. I thought I’d be judged.

No judgement at all. I’d suggest talking therapy — you can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies, and new mums are seen quickly — and I’d like to let your health visitor know so she can support you too. Is that okay with you?
model.why: Shares the plan and seeks consent before involving the health visitor

model.text: Yes. That would help.

If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, feel suddenly very different or confused, or can’t cope, call us the same day, or 111 or 999 out of hours. I’ll see you again in two weeks with the blood results to see how you’re doing.
model.why: Specific risk safety-net and booked review

model.text: Okay. Two weeks.
What will you take away from today?
The hair will come back, bloods for iron and thyroid, and that it’s okay to not be okay — I’m getting help.
That’s exactly it. You came about your hair, but I’m glad we looked after you too.

social.t: She feels she lacks help and doesn’t want to be a burden. Explore who could help, and local mother and baby support.
Postnatal body changes and loss of the old sense of self are common drivers of distress; name them as valid.

legal.t: If she is employed and on maternity leave, return-to-work timing can be discussed; a fit note is only relevant if illness affects work after leave ends.
No current risk to the baby is disclosed. Asking about thoughts of harm is routine; significant risk would need same-day action and liaison with the health visitor and perinatal team.

professional.t: Seek her agreement before informing the health visitor (GMC Confidentiality, 2017); explain it is for support, not surveillance.
Check any medicine against the BNF for breastfeeding before prescribing, including antidepressants if later needed.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral, perinatal priority), health visitor, perinatal mental health team for severe illness, PANDAS Foundation and Mind for peer support.

redFlags: Thoughts of suicide, self-harm or harming the baby
Rapid change in mental state, confusion or psychotic symptoms postnatally
Scalp redness, soreness or patches — not typical postpartum shedding
Symptoms of anaemia or thyroid dysfunction
psychosocial: First baby, 4 months, exhausted; feeding hard work
Feels unsupported and fears being a burden
Body image and loss of identity
ice: Concern: falling apart; not recognising herself
Expectation: to know if the hair will stop — and to be heard

playbook.diagnosis: “The hair loss is the normal shed that happens after a baby, and it recovers. What worries me more is how low and anxious you’ve been — that sounds like postnatal depression and anxiety, which is common and treatable.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “During pregnancy your hair gets a ‘pause’ on falling out. After the birth the pause ends and months of hair fall together. It’s a catch-up, not baldness.”

management.reflectIce: “You called it the last straw — so let’s deal with the hair, and then with everything underneath it.”
management.psychosocial: Validate exhaustion and body-image change; look for practical support; involve the health visitor with consent.
sharedPlan: Reassurance with timeline for postpartum telogen effluvium
FBC, ferritin, TFTs; treat deficiency, dose per BNF
NHS Talking Therapies self-referral and health visitor support; perinatal team if severe
safetyNet: Same-day contact, 111 or 999 for thoughts of harm, sudden change or confusion
Review in two weeks with results and mood

pitfalls.intro: The hair is a ticket. Most candidates handle it well and then close the consultation, missing the postnatal depression and anxiety she has been waiting to be asked about.

items.fail: Reassuring about postpartum shedding and ending there.
items.why: “Does not identify the patient’s underlying agenda.” The mood symptoms are the case.
items.fix: Follow “falling apart” with the Whooley and GAD-2 questions.

items.fail: Asking about mood but not about thoughts of harm to herself or the baby.
items.why: NICE CG192 expects direct risk questions once mood symptoms are present; omitting them is unsafe.
items.fix: “I ask everyone this: any thoughts of harming yourself or the baby?”

items.fail: No blood tests, or a large unfocused panel.
items.why: Delivery blood loss and postpartum thyroiditis are real contributors; over-investigation is not.
items.fix: FBC, ferritin and TFTs — and explain why each.

items.why: Normalising dismisses her; she already fears judgement.
items.fix: “Lots of mums do feel this — and it’s treatable, so let’s get you support.”

items.fail: Informing the health visitor without asking her.
items.why: Acting without consent undermines trust at the moment she has disclosed.
items.fix: Explain the purpose and ask: “Would it be okay if I let your health visitor know?”

items.fail: No clear route for help if things get worse.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name thoughts of harm, sudden change or confusion; same day, 111, 999; review in two weeks.

timeMap.d: She calls the hair trivial and then says she is falling apart. Name both and set a two-part agenda.
Timing, pattern, scalp symptoms, delivery blood loss, feeding, thyroid symptoms.
Follow “falling apart”. Whooley and GAD-2, then risk to self and baby. Support, body image.
Postpartum shed with mechanism and timeline. FBC, ferritin, TFTs. Name postnatal depression and anxiety; Talking Therapies, health visitor with consent.
Same-day, 111, 999 routes. Review in two weeks. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Reassures about the hair and ends the consultation; never asks about mood despite “falling apart”; no thyroid or iron check; or suggests minoxidil while breastfeeding.
wordPics.pass: Reassures accurately about postpartum shedding, checks FBC, ferritin and TFTs, asks the mood questions including risk, and arranges support and follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: refuses the “trivial” framing at the start; screens mood with the Whooley and GAD-2 questions and asks directly about harm to self and baby; validates body-image change without judgement; seeks consent to involve the health visitor; names what she has in plain words; she leaves feeling looked after as a person.

avoid.dont: “Oh, that’s completely normal after a baby — it’ll grow back.” (end of consultation)
avoid.instead: “The hair will grow back — and I heard you say you’re falling apart. Can we talk about you?”
avoid.why: Reassuring the ticket and closing misses the real case.

avoid.instead: “You said you don’t enjoy anything and worry all the time — that sounds like more than tiredness.”
avoid.why: Normalising dismisses symptoms of postnatal depression and anxiety.

avoid.instead: “This type of shed recovers by itself; let’s check your iron and thyroid.”
avoid.why: Not indicated for postpartum shedding and not advised when breastfeeding.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; refused the “trivial” framing and set an agenda covering both the hair and her wellbeing.
Birth and blood loss, feeding (relevant to prescribing), support at home, reluctance to be a burden, body image and loss of identity.
Followed “falling apart”, “last straw” and “nothing about my body feels like mine”.
Idea (hair loss is trivial but distressing); concern (falling apart, not recognising herself); expectation (will it stop — and to be heard).
Scalp symptoms asked; FBC, ferritin and TFTs for delivery blood loss and postpartum thyroiditis; no over-investigation.
Postpartum telogen effluvium versus patchy or scarring loss; iron deficiency, postpartum thyroiditis; postnatal depression and anxiety.
Whooley and GAD-2 questions, then direct questions about thoughts of self-harm and harm to the baby (NICE CG192).
Named postpartum telogen effluvium and probable postnatal depression and anxiety, both clearly and without blame.
Reassurance with timeline; tests; NHS Talking Therapies self-referral; health visitor involvement with consent.
Feeding status considered in treatment choices (no minoxidil); iron replacement if deficient; thyroid follow-up.
Same-day, 111 and 999 routes for risk or rapid change; review in two weeks with results and mood.

social.t: She feels she lacks help and doesn’t want to be a burden. Explore who could help, and local mother and baby support.
Postnatal body changes and loss of the old sense of self are common drivers of distress; name them as valid.

legal.t: If she is employed and on maternity leave, return-to-work timing can be discussed; a fit note is only relevant if illness affects work after leave ends.
No current risk to the baby is disclosed. Asking about thoughts of harm is routine; significant risk would need same-day action and liaison with the health visitor and perinatal team.

professional.t: Seek her agreement before informing the health visitor (GMC Confidentiality, 2017); explain it is for support, not surveillance.
Check any medicine against the BNF for breastfeeding before prescribing, including antidepressants if later needed.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral, perinatal priority), health visitor, perinatal mental health team for severe illness, PANDAS Foundation and Mind for peer support.

redFlags: Thoughts of suicide, self-harm or harming the baby
Rapid change in mental state, confusion or psychotic symptoms postnatally
Scalp redness, soreness or patches — not typical postpartum shedding
Symptoms of anaemia or thyroid dysfunction
psychosocial: First baby, 4 months, exhausted; feeding hard work
Feels unsupported and fears being a burden
Body image and loss of identity
ice: Concern: falling apart; not recognising herself
Expectation: to know if the hair will stop — and to be heard

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The hair loss is the normal shed that happens after a baby, and it recovers. What worries me more is how low and anxious you’ve been — that sounds like postnatal depression and anxiety, which is common and treatable.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “During pregnancy your hair gets a ‘pause’ on falling out. After the birth the pause ends and months of hair fall together. It’s a catch-up, not baldness.”

management.reflectIce: “You called it the last straw — so let’s deal with the hair, and then with everything underneath it.”
management.psychosocial: Validate exhaustion and body-image change; look for practical support; involve the health visitor with consent.
sharedPlan: Reassurance with timeline for postpartum telogen effluvium
FBC, ferritin, TFTs; treat deficiency, dose per BNF
NHS Talking Therapies self-referral and health visitor support; perinatal team if severe
safetyNet: Same-day contact, 111 or 999 for thoughts of harm, sudden change or confusion
Review in two weeks with results and mood

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The hair is a ticket. Most candidates handle it well and then close the consultation, missing the postnatal depression and anxiety she has been waiting to be asked about.

items.fail: Reassuring about postpartum shedding and ending there.
items.why: “Does not identify the patient’s underlying agenda.” The mood symptoms are the case.
items.fix: Follow “falling apart” with the Whooley and GAD-2 questions.

items.fail: Asking about mood but not about thoughts of harm to herself or the baby.
items.why: NICE CG192 expects direct risk questions once mood symptoms are present; omitting them is unsafe.
items.fix: “I ask everyone this: any thoughts of harming yourself or the baby?”

items.fail: No blood tests, or a large unfocused panel.
items.why: Delivery blood loss and postpartum thyroiditis are real contributors; over-investigation is not.
items.fix: FBC, ferritin and TFTs — and explain why each.

items.why: Normalising dismisses her; she already fears judgement.
items.fix: “Lots of mums do feel this — and it’s treatable, so let’s get you support.”

items.fail: Informing the health visitor without asking her.
items.why: Acting without consent undermines trust at the moment she has disclosed.
items.fix: Explain the purpose and ask: “Would it be okay if I let your health visitor know?”

items.fail: No clear route for help if things get worse.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name thoughts of harm, sudden change or confusion; same day, 111, 999; review in two weeks.
